Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette: Two years ago, forty-one-year-old Arjun's life fractured during a night that still played behind his eyelids as sharp, unblinking photographs. He remembered the kitchen in vivid, unyielding snapshots: the glass shattering, his partner's face contorted, the heavy scent of bourbon soaking into the curtains. When the arguments began, the words spilled out in a frantic, incomprehensible mix of Hindi and English. That same nauseating sensation instantly pulled his mind back to the frozen snapshots of the assault, replaying the violence in his head. When the scent of alcohol first hit him that night, he was immediately certain he had failed his marriage and that his own judgment was fundamentally unreliable. The terror of those moments refused to fade, and each time the photographs of the violence surfaced in his mind, his shoulders would lock and his breathing would shallow, as if the threat were still present. Reliving the betrayal with such visceral clarity only deepened his conviction that he could no longer trust himself to navigate life safely. As weeks bled into months, the physical toll became his new baseline. His body would brace and tense before he could consciously name the danger, his pulse spiking at dropped keys or slamming doors. This constant state of alertness kept his nervous system on high alert, which in turn forced his thoughts back to the traumatic event, replaying the violent sequences until he felt sick again. The constant startle response and inability to sleep eroded his confidence, reinforcing the belief that he had lost his capacity to protect those he loved. Believing he was broken beyond repair only heightened his physical tension, convincing him that danger was still closing in. His perpetually reactive body soon began interpreting neutral cues as imminent danger, so that everyday sounds and smells would instantly activate his distress. He stopped resting his head on the pillow after dark, convinced that drifting off would leave him defenseless if the past returned. Now, at his architectural firm, Arjun navigated a carefully curated routine to keep the past at bay. During a site walkthrough at a mixed-use development, a contractor laughed loudly over a radio tuned to a regional station. The overlapping speech and the sudden wave of nausea sent his heart hammering against his ribs before he could even identify the danger. He excused himself to the restroom, gripping the sink as his breath came in short, shallow gasps. When he finally stepped back into the conference room for the evening design review, a senior partner offered a glass of scotch to toast a milestone. Arjun realized he could no longer sit through the presentation; his hands trembled as he tried to unroll the blueprints, certain that if he stayed, he would lose control entirely. He had failed to uphold his role as a steady provider and partner, and the weight of that belief made the physical reactions feel like permanent evidence of his inadequacy. The cycle tightened relentlessly across his career and marriage. A missed deadline due to his prolonged absence from client meetings quietly eroded his standing at the firm, while his wife's exhausted sighs at his sudden flinches made him feel like a stranger in his own home. Three months ago, she packed a bag and left, unable to watch him shrink into a ghost. What finally brought Arjun to the clinic was a morning when he stood in his kitchen, paralyzed by the smell of his wife's coffee, convinced he was about to collapse again. He did not want to lose his career or his children to a past he could not outrun. He hoped, however faintly, that someone might help him untangle the fear from the facts so he could finally exhale.
